content.title: About
content.content: Baby Toddler Bananas, Stage 1 are soft, fully ripe bananas prepared especially for infants aged 6 to 12 months. They are rich in natural sugars, vitamins and minerals, easily digestible and ideal for first foods.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bananas are one of the first fruits typically introduced into a baby’s diet.
They contain tryptophan, which supports serotonin production and mood regulation.
Bananas are easy to digest and rarely cause allergic reactions.
Unlike many fruits, these bananas are pre‑peeled and cut, so no extra preparation is needed.
Their natural sweetness often replaces added sugars in infant meals.

items.title: Rich in potassium
items.content: Potassium supports normal heart and muscle function and helps regulate fluid balance.

items.title: Source of vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 aids nervous system development and neurotransmitter synthesis.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts immunity and enhances iron absorption.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Soluble fiber in bananas helps regulate bowel movements and prevents constipation.

items.title: Low allergen potential
items.content: Bananas rarely trigger allergic reactions, making them a safe first‑food choice.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: For infants under 12 months, bananas should be pureed or very finely mashed to avoid choking.

items.title: Possible sensitivity to fruit sugars
items.content: Some babies may experience loose stools if given too much fruit sugar.

items.title: Monitor ripeness
items.content: Over‑ripe bananas can become overly soft and sticky, making feeding difficult.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Peel the banana, mash it with a fork to a smooth puree or blend it. If needed, add a little breast milk or formula to achieve the desired consistency.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store bananas in the refrigerator in an airtight container for up to 24 hours. For longer storage, freeze portioned pieces and thaw before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Chow mein (stir‑fried noodles) and chop suey (a mix of vegetables, meat and noodles) are popular Chinese‑style dishes often served in fast‑casual restaurants. The NS version uses lean meat (such as chicken, turkey or beef) and wheat‑based noodles (item 1505). The dishes are cooked quickly over high heat, preserving the crunch of the vegetables and the aroma of the spices.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chow mein arrived in the United States in the early 20th century and became an icon of Chinese street food.
The term "chop suey" literally means "assorted leftovers" and originally referred to a dish made from whatever ingredients were on hand.
Noodle 1505 is made from wheat flour and has a medium thickness, making it ideal for rapid stir‑frying.
Traditional recipes often include soy sauce, ginger, garlic and sesame oil.
The NS (no soy) variant may omit soy sauce for those with soy allergies.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Lean meat provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and vegetables supply B1, B2, B6 and niacin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains fiber
items.content: Vegetables such as carrots, cabbage and bell pepper add dietary fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Using lean meat and a modest amount of oil keeps the dish relatively low‑calorie.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Ginger, garlic and the vegetables provide antioxidants that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Wheat‑based noodles contain gluten, which can be problematic for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce and pre‑made seasoning packets are often high in salt; those with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Cross‑contamination risk
items.content: Restaurant preparation may expose the dish to common allergens such as peanuts or shellfish.

items.title: Meat cooking safety
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor pathogenic bacteria; ensure it is cooked to a safe internal temperature.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, typically in a deep bowl or plate. Squeeze fresh lime, sprinkle chopped green onion or add chili to taste. For extra crunch, top with toasted nuts such as cashews or peanuts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Chow mein or chop suey is best enjoyed immediately. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. When reheating, add a splash of oil to restore noodle crispness.

pasta-with-cream-sauce-and-added-vegetab.title: Pasta with Cream Sauce and Added Vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: Pasta with cream sauce and added vegetables is a home recipe (3620) that combines cooked pasta, a smooth cream sauce, and a variety of fresh vegetables such as broccoli, carrots, bell pepper, and zucchini. The dish is flavorful, quick to prepare, and suitable for lunch or dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cream sauce is often made from heavy cream, butter, and Parmesan, giving the dish a velvety texture.
Vegetables retain most of their vitamins when lightly sautéed or blanched before being mixed into the pasta.
Cooking pasta "al dente" helps it hold onto the sauce better, creating a more harmonious bite.
A homemade recipe allows you to control salt and fat levels, making it healthier than many store‑bought sauces.
Traditional Italian cuisine often uses fettuccine or penne for creamy sauces like this.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Durum wheat pasta provides B1, B2, and niacin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Vegetables such as broccoli and carrots add fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: The cream sauce with Parmesan and vegetables supplies antioxidants (vitamin E, carotenoids) that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports bone health
items.content: Cheese and cream are sources of calcium and phosphorus, essential for strong bones.

items.title: Balanced protein‑carbohydrate combo
items.content: Pasta provides complex carbs while the sauce and vegetables contribute plant‑based and dairy proteins.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Cream sauce can be calorie‑dense and contain saturated fat; portion control is recommended.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Cream and cheese may cause discomfort for those with lactose intolerance; plant‑based alternatives can be used.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to dairy should avoid the traditional sauce or substitute with non‑dairy options.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Parmesan adds salt; reduce added salt if you need to limit sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pasta hot, garnished with fresh herbs (parsley, basil) and extra grated Parmesan if desired. It pairs well with a light side salad or whole‑grain bread.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat gently, adding a splash of milk or cream to restore the sauce's creaminess.

content.title: About
content.content: Popcorn Microwave NFS (2985) is a ready‑to‑cook grain snack designed for microwave ovens. The bag contains pre‑selected corn kernels coated with a flavorful seasoning that pop in 2–3 minutes, creating light, crunchy pieces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Popcorn is the only type of corn whose kernels explode when heated due to high internal moisture.
Microwave popcorn appeared in the 1980s and quickly became popular for its convenience and speed.
In the United States more than 13 billion servings of popcorn are consumed each year, a large share of which is microwave popcorn.
NFS popcorn features a proprietary spice blend developed with food technologists.
Each serving provides about 100 kcal, making it a popular light snack.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike oil‑popped popcorn, microwave popcorn is prepared without added oil, reducing overall fat content.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Corn kernels are rich in dietary fiber, which supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Popcorn contains polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: The carbohydrates in popcorn are quickly digestible, providing a rapid source of energy.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Corn is naturally gluten‑free, making this product suitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Some flavored varieties contain a notable amount of salt; those monitoring sodium intake should choose low‑salt options.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Although rare, corn allergy can occur and may manifest as skin reactions or breathing difficulties.

items.title: Burn risk
items.content: Hot steam released from the bag after cooking can cause burns; allow a few minutes to cool before opening.

items.title: Additive content
items.content: Certain flavors may include artificial flavorings and preservatives; select versions with minimal ingredients if this matters to you.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Place the bag in the microwave and cook for 2–3 minutes, then carefully open the bag to let the steam escape. Eat the popcorn as is, or add grated cheese, extra spices, or a small amount of melted butter to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened bag in a dry, cool place away from moisture. After opening, transfer any remaining popcorn to an airtight container to keep it crunchy and prevent it from absorbing odors.

content.title: About
content.content: The Seafood Salad Sandwich is a sandwich that layers a salad made from boiled seafood (shrimp, crab meat, mussels), vegetables, and a light mayo‑based dressing between slices of bread. It is popular in coastal cafés and restaurants, combining the freshness of the sea with a crunchy bun.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first seafood salad recipes appeared in the United States in the 1970s as part of the “seafood salad” trend.
The sandwich is usually served cold, but it can be lightly toasted for extra crunch.
Lemon juice and fresh dill are commonly added for extra aroma.
Variations may include avocado, cucumber, or a splash of soy sauce.
It packs well in cling film for picnics and lunchboxes.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Shrimp and crab provide omega‑3s that support heart health and reduce inflammation.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: Seafood offers easily digestible protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with many meat sandwiches, this version contains little saturated fat.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Seafood is a good source of B12 and B6, which help maintain nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals: zinc and selenium
items.content: Zinc and selenium support immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to shrimp, mussels, or other shellfish.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared seafood is often salted; people watching their sodium intake should choose low‑salt options.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Improper storage can lead to bacterial growth, so keep seafood chilled at all times.

items.title: Added ingredients
items.content: Commercial mayo may contain added sugars and preservatives, which some prefer to avoid.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the sandwich in half and enjoy it cold or lightly warmed in a toaster. It pairs well with a simple side salad, fries, or fresh veggie sticks. Optional toppings include mustard or tartar sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the assembled sandwich in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. If the seafood salad is prepared separately, keep it chilled to prevent the bread from becoming soggy.
